key.Fingerprint\\u0060) established a verified root and wrote \\u0060node.yaml\\u0060 regardless of whether the project\\u0027s own \\u0060members/\\u0060 folder already belonged to someone else; only the genesis MEMBER write ever backed off (\\u0060HasAnyAsync\\u0060), so the newcomer ended up a solo, self-certified owner on a shared repository, publishing issues and opening pull requests under their own login while every message they sent was dropped by the team as \\u0060SenderNotVouched\\u0060. **The rule.** A join never mints an owner root on a ledger that already has genesis: \\u0060ProjectJoinCommand.RunAsync\\u0060 now checks, before any key is generated or any ledger byte is written, whether this join\\u0027s own no-\\u0060--owner\\u0060, no-\\u0060--invite\\u0060 fallback would self-establish a root here \\u2014 because this install claims no root of its own yet (\\u0060OwnerAggregate.RootFingerprint\\u0060 is null), or because an earlier join of a *different* project already self-established one and this node\\u0027s own key (read from the already-loaded node aggregate, no key touched or generated to make this check) equals it. Either way it asks the ledger\\u0027s own \\u0060members/\\u0060 folder (\\u0060ILedger.HasAnyAsync\\u0060) rather than trusting the local fallback alone, and \\u2014 when that folder already names this exact fingerprint as genesis \\u2014 treats it as an ordinary re-join rather than a defer, since that is this same identity\\u0027s own project, not a second owner\\u0027s. A non-empty folder naming someone else defers: no \\u0060root.yaml\\u0060, no \\u0060node.yaml\\u0060, no \\u0060OwnerRootClaimed\\u0060 event, and one sentence naming the existing owner (their login when this install\\u0027s own \\u0060OwnerDetails\\u0060 already knows one for that fingerprint, else the bare fingerprint) and that joining needs an invite from them. An empty folder \\u2014 genuinely this project\\u0027s first join \\u2014 is unaffected and still establishes the root exactly as before; the identical fallback is unaffected too whenever an explicit \\u0060--owner\\u0060 or \\u0060--invite\\u0060 already says whose root this join claims, since there is nothing left for this gate to defer. (Fix round, same task: the first cut of this rule checked only the null-root case, so an install that already owned one project could still self-write a second owner\\u0027s root.yaml and node.yaml into another project\\u0027s ledger by the same route this incident describes \\u2014 independent pre-PR review, cycle 1, adversarial lens.) **The prompt.** When this process is attached to a real terminal, the same call then asks for the invite token on the spot (\\u0060AnsiConsole.Prompt\\u0060, seamed behind a \\u0060Func\\u003Cstring?\\u003E?\\u0060 so every scenario is testable against the fake ledger with no real console): a pasted token falls through into the ordinary \\u0060--invite\\u0060 path in the same invocation and reports exactly as \\u0060h9k project join --invite\\u0060 does --invite \\u003Ctoken\\u003E\\u0060, and exits successfully with the registration kept. \\u0060h9k project add\\u0060 now accepts \\u0060--invite \\u003Ctoken\\u003E\\u0060 too, threaded straight into join yet\\u0022) answers \\u0022is this install a recognized member of this project\\u0027s own ledger yet\\u0022 from purely local, already-replicated state \\u2014 this install\\u0027s own claimed root fingerprint and the project\\u0027s own local \\u0060Members\\u0060 mirror, kept current by \\u0060MemberVouched\\u0060 replication \\u2014 never a live ledger fetch. \\u0060h9k project show\\u0060 gains a \\u0060Joined\\u0060 row and \\u0060h9k status\\u0060 gains a line, both reading \\u0060not joined yet\\u0060 and pointing at the plain join command for exactly this state, since only a live ledger read inside \\u0060h9k project join\\u0060 itself can tell whether an invite is actually needed. **The repair path.** A second, orphaned root an earlier build already minted for a newcomer before this shipped is retired exactly the way an explicit \\u0060--owner\\u0060/\\u0060--invite\\u0060 join already retires any self-created root that turns out to be wrong (\\u0060RetireSelfRootEverywhereAsync\\u0060, unchanged by this task): running \\u0060h9k project join \\u003Cproject\\u003E --invite \\u003Ctoken\\u003E\\u0060 with the real owner\\u0027s own invite is the repair, for anyone who joined before this shipped. **Tests.** All against the fake ledger the existing join tests already use, no repository or remote touched: an existing genesis with no local root claim writes nothing and names the owner (by login when known, by fingerprint otherwise); a terminal answered with a token runs the ordinary invite path in the same call; a terminal answered with enter prints the exact command; a non-interactive run never prompts and prints the identical command; an empty ledger still establishes the root exactly as before; \\u0060h9k project add --invite\\u0060 passes the token through to the ordinary invite path. The same fix round adds: an install that already self-established a root on one project defers rather than self-writing into a second project someone else owns; a re-join of a project this same pull brings a task\\u0027s whole story with it: the answer carries the task\\u0027s run streams, the platform asks for the dependencies a landed task names and this node does not hold, a closed request is re-asked and \\u0060--again\\u0060 clears one still outstanding, and the short id off a board row resolves through the project\\u0027s ledger.** Why: task 9eb5b245, from two observations. On 2026-09-19 Windows queued a broadcast for ec35ceca\\u0027s stream at 13:40, the Mac declined it at 13:41, and the 23:36 re-run was told the old request was still on its way; the decline had closed nothing on that build, and nothing distinguished \\u0022one was asked\\u0022 from \\u0022one is in flight\\u0022 anyway. On 2026-09-21 the Mac pulled 3727884f and it landed in about two and a half minutes as Delivered with laps 0 and sessions 0, because the answer carried the task stream and not the run streams hanging off it, while the answering node had that same task Done. **A closed request is not an ask in flight.** \\u0060StreamRequestDecision\\u0060 is the whole re-ask rule as a pure function over the requests a node already holds for one stream: no prior request queues a first ask, an outstanding one suppresses the ask and says so, \\u0060--again\\u0060 closes that one out and queues a replacement, and every other case (answered, declined, exhausted, itself superseded) is a re-ask that reports itself as one. A supersede is recorded as \\u0060EventCatchUpRequest.SupersededAt\\u0060 and \\u0060SupersededByRequestId\\u0060, never as \\u0060AnsweredAt\\u0060: nothing answered it, and recording a supersede as an answer would claim an observation nobody made. \\u0060--again\\u0060 is therefore also the only lever that clears a request minted before v0.10.5, which the inbox of the day left standing because it applied a decline to a candidate cascade alone (request 01a0bac1 of 2026-09-19 is that shape). An automatic caller passes a re-mint cooldown and a human\\u0027s own ask never does, the same shape \\u0060RequestGapFillAsync\\u0060 already uses: a human asking twice means it. **A stream ask answers with the task\\u0027s runs too.** \\u0060EventCatchUpResponder\\u0060 widens a \\u0060ForStreamId\\u0060 request to that task\\u0027s own run streams (\\u0060RunListItem.TaskId\\u0060, the only join there is, since a run\\u0027s stream id is not derivable from its task\\u0027s), each whole and each genesis first, which the existing single scan ordered by the answering node\\u0027s own global sequence gives free. A run stream id asked for directly answers as itself, because no run\\u0027s \\u0060TaskId\\u0060 is a run id, and that is exactly what \\u0060h9k task pull \\u003Crun-id\\u003E\\u0060 should mean. **The platform asks for the dependencies it can fetch.** \\u0060TaskDecider.Assign\\u0060 refuses an assignment whose blockers this node holds no document for, which for a task pulled from a peer is a refusal over a stream the platform could have fetched itself. \\u0060TaskDependencyCatchUp\\u0060 mints that ask: one broadcast per missing blocked-by or stacked-on id, at the moment a task lands in \\u0060EventReplicationInbox\\u0060, deduplicated per stream and bounded to the project whose landing triggered it, because the project of a stream this node does not hold is unknowable and a request has to name one. Recursive by arrival rather than by guessing, since a stream that is not here has no edges to read: the walk descends through dependencies this node actually holds, and each landing runs it again, so a chain arrives one hop per landing. A dependency whose stream is here only as a tail is skipped rather than asked for, since that answer could only be refused on arrival. \\u0060h9k status\\u0060 names each such ask and whose dependency it is, and \\u0060h9k task pull\\u0060 on a task already here makes the same asks for whatever it is still missing, which is the lever for a task that landed before this existed. **The short id is what a human actually has.** The full id lived only on the node that held the task, which is the node they are not sitting at, so \\u0060h9k task pull\\u0060 resolves a fragment against this node\\u0027s own tasks first and then against the project\\u0027s ledger records, and defaults \\u0060--project\\u0060 to the one project whose ledger names the task. The existing refusals stand where neither holds. That ledger read is the one time this command touches git, and it is skipped entirely for a full id on a node with one eligible project or with \\u0060--project\\u0060 named. **Tests.** Four unit suites, none touching a repository, a remote, or a branch (Brian, 2026-09-13): the re-ask rule over every prior-request shape including the pre-v0.10.5 one; the dependency walk (blockers, a stacked parent, recursion, a diamond, a cycle, a foreign project, and the assign refusal naming exactly what the walk asks for); the ledger lookup by short id, head fragment and full id across two projects; and the stream set a task ask serves. Four integration tests carry the parts a database decides: the re-ask and supersede sequence end to end, a short id resolving and defaulting its project, a dependency ask minted for a task already held, and a responder answer carrying a run stream whole with its genesis first. \\u0060dotnet build\\u0060 and \\u0060dotnet test\\u0060 pass. **Does this block the later vision?** No: every piece here is local bookkeeping and one more thing an existing answer carries, and nothing touches the P2P identity layer (\\u00A716 #38-#58).\u0022,\u0022OriginIncident\u0022:null,\u0022Supersedes\u0022:[],\u0022Provenance\u0022:{\u0022RecordedByOwnerId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5a50-7368-b048-72bcfee948bf\u0022,\u0022RunId\u0022:null,\u0022TaskId\u0022:null,\u0022Attendance\u0022:\u0022Unobserved\u0022,\u0022IsFromRun\u0022:false},\u0022RecordedAt\u0022:\u00222026-09-22T13:15:38.803749\u002B00:00\u0022,\u0022LegacyId\u0022:\u0022Decisions Log #258\u0022}","originEventId":"80e3da96-dce9-4725-bbb6-82032f78323b","originSequence":59057,"originNodeId":"01a00d41-5b80-753d-a3f1-070b25e490e4","originOwnerRootFingerprint":"c8f5c85900dac9911ce1ada43484dc7bf91a2a3e86efa8812d9f84cfd25bf2ac","originAt":"2026-09-22T13:15:39.711033+00:00","originProjectId":"01a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71"},{"streamId":"01a0c941-fb35-7555-8fc8-1b7cc95c970f","eventTypeName":"Hall9k.Domain.Features.Decision.DecisionRecorded","eventDataJson":"{\u0022Id\u0022:\u002201a0c941-fb35-7555-8fc8-1b7cc95c970f\u0022,\u0022Scope\u0022:\u0022Project\u0022,\u0022ScopeId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71\u0022,\u0022Statement\u0022:\u0022**A stream this node holds only the tail of completes on its own: the sweep mints one bounded broadcast ask per held tail, and every decline is recorded by node and time and shown on the status line, so no human has to run \\u0060h9k task pull\\u0060 for work the fleet already holds.** Why: split from 9eb5b245 on Brian\\u0027s ruling 2026-09-21 after the challenge session; the automatic-completion half of that draft, built right after 805f6986 (the repair that frees partial streams) because the held-tail ask is what finishes a freed stream without a human. Origin incident (2026-09-19 13:40): Windows queued a broadcast events-request for ec35ceca\\u0027s stream, the Mac answered \\u0060events-unavailable\\u0060 at 13:41, and at 23:36 a re-run of \\u0060h9k task add --from-issue 447\\u0060 was told the old ask was still on its way. The challenge session\\u0027s finding is what scoped this entry: main has closed a broadcast on a decline since 717c5805 (2026-09-19 15:40, shipped in v0.10.5), so that refusal was a pre-v0.10.5 document, and the remaining gaps were the bookkeeping and the asking. **A decline is an observation, not a summary.** \\u0060EventCatchUpRequest.Declines\\u0060 is a list of \\u0060EventCatchUpDecline\\u0060 (declining node, the time this node read it, the reason verbatim), one entry per declining node, kept at the first decline that node sent: a peer cannot make \\u0022I hold nothing\\u0022 more true by repeating it, and a re-delivered envelope must not grow the list without bound. \\u0060DeclinedReason\\u0060 stays beside the list rather than being derived from it, because a request document written by an older build carries that string and nothing else, and deriving a node and a time from a bare reason would be inventing provenance. A decline is recorded even when the request has already ended: on a broadcast every member answers and the first answer closes the ask, so dropping the rest would let \\u0060h9k status\\u0060 name one declining node out of five and read as \\u0022one peer could not help\\u0022 rather than \\u0022nobody could\\u0022. **What closed a request is recorded, never reconstructed.** \\u0060ClosedByDecline\\u0060 holds the one decline that actually ended the request, either a broadcast\\u0027s first, or the last ranked candidate\\u0027s, which exhausts the cascade. It is set by the inbox rather than inside \\u0060AdvanceToNextCandidateAsync\\u0060, which a silent timeout also calls and which would have to guess. The alternative considered and rejected was matching a decline\\u0027s own timestamp against \\u0060AnsweredAt\\u0060: that cannot tell a cascade closed by its last decline from one whose next candidate answered for real. A document written before this field exists leaves it null and prints nothing, which is the honest outcome rather than a plausible one. **The held-tail ask is bounded four ways, and the bounds are the feature.** \\u0060EventCatchUpCoordinator.PlanHeldTailAsks\\u0060 is pure, and every rule lives there: a stream already at \\u0060MaxHeldTailAttempts\\u0060 (three) is never asked again; a stream whose oldest held record is younger than one sweep interval is left alone; a stream with an outstanding request is not asked twice; and a stream asked inside the re-mint cooldown waits, whatever became of that ask. The per-sweep cap of ten is applied last, to whatever survived, oldest hold first, because the cap has to choose and \\u0022waiting longest\\u0022 is the only order that starves nothing. The settle window is read off \\u0060DaemonOptions.MessageIdlePollMaxSeconds\\u0060, the longest this sweep ever waits between ticks, so a hold that outlives it is a hold at least one full sweep failed to fix; erring long costs one sweep of patience, and erring short asks the project for history it is in the middle of sending. The cooldown is \\u0060EventCatchUpRequestTimeout\\u0060 unchanged, the same value and the same shape \\u0060RequestGapFillAsync\\u0060 already reuses, and it is load-bearing here for a sharper reason than there: a decline closes a broadcast the instant it is read and an answer that lands without the genesis closes one just as fast, so \\u0022not outstanding\\u0022 arrives within seconds either way and the cooldown is the only thing between that and a fresh ask every tick. **Three attempts, and the count lives on the held records.** Not on the request documents: the held records are what the sweep already reads and what vanish the moment the genesis lands, so a stream whose tail completed leaves no counter behind to keep re-reading. That only holds while a re-delivery cannot clear the counter, and a re-delivery is exactly what a held-tail ask gets answered with: a peer holding the same tail and not the genesis serves that tail again. \\u0060EventReplicationInbox\\u0060 therefore leaves an already-held record exactly as it is rather than storing over it, since \\u0060Store\\u0060 on the same origin event id is an upsert \\u2014 it reset \\u0060CatchUpAttempts\\u0060 to zero, cleared \\u0060LastCatchUpAskedAt\\u0060 and \\u0060CatchUpGivenUp\\u0060, and refreshed \\u0060HeldAt\\u0060 on every answer, so the stop never engaged for the very shape it exists for and the stream was asked about again every cooldown for as long as the node ran. The mark is per record and the verdict is per stream (\\u0060HeldTailStreams.GivenUpStreamIdsAsync\\u0060), because a held record arriving after the stop carries a count of zero of its own and would otherwise put its stream back in rotation and restart the whole cycle on every later arrival, and for a tail that keeps growing behind a genesis nobody holds, that is exactly the unbounded loop the stop exists to prevent. Given up is not a verdict on the tail: it still replays if the genesis ever turns up, and what stopped is only this node asking. The mark lands on the sweep that declines to mint a fourth ask, never on the one that mints the third: stamping it at the mint had \\u0060h9k status\\u0060 reporting a stream given up while its own ask was still in flight and might yet be answered. So \\u0060PlanHeldTailAsks\\u0060 returns the give-ups as a second list, gated by the same settle, outstanding and cooldown guards the asks are \\u2014 a stream given up on is one that would be asked again now if it had an ask left \\u2014 and capped the same way, because the caller pays one stream-state read per stream it acts on whichever way it acts. The shape that produces a genuinely unanswerable tail, from the 2026-09-21 evidence (42 held records over 14 Mac-origin run streams, origin sequences 7009 to 21085, tails served without their \\u0060RunDispatched\\u0060), is most likely a genesis event carrying a retired event type name the current build\\u0027s \\u0060EventScopeRegistry\\u0060 does not know, which \\u0060EventCatchUpResponder.AnswerAsync\\u0060 skips silently. No number of asks produces that, which is why the stop is a stop rather than a longer wait. **Naming, not a human\\u0027s hand, is what lifts a peer\\u0027s switch-on floor.** \\u0060EventsRequestRecord.IsExplicitAsk\\u0060 read as \\u0022a human explicitly asked for this\\u0022 because until now the only named-stream requests came from the CLI. The held-tail ask is minted by a sweep and names one stream, so it lifts the exclusion, and it has to: the genesis events those 14 held tails were waiting on sat at Mac origin sequences 7009 to 21085, below that node\\u0027s own switch-on point at 30084, so an ask that kept the exclusion could never have been answered at all. Naming is still the right rule rather than a coincidence, because a request that names one stream asks a peer to complete history that already partly travelled here and can reach nothing else, which is precisely the case the exclusion was never meant to strand. The three places that stated the old reading (the request record\\u0027s own doc, \\u0060IsExplicitAsk\\u0060, and \\u0060EventCatchUpResponder.AnswerAsync\\u0060\\u0027s comment) now state this one, found by this branch\\u0027s own self-review rather than in review. **One rule needs a store to state.** A held record whose stream actually exists locally is the residue of a replay that never ran, not a missing genesis: the inbox\\u0027s deferred replay is driven by an in-memory set of the streams a genesis started this read, so a read that starts a stream and then throws on a later record loses it, and the retry finds the genesis already deduped and never names the stream again. Such a stream is neither asked about nor given up on. The sweep returns it (\\u0060HeldTailSweepResult.StreamsToReplay\\u0060) and the daemon hands it straight to \\u0060EventReplicationInbox.ReplayHeldTailAsync\\u0060, which applies each held record and deletes it, because nothing else ever will: merely skipping it left the records there for good, spending a slot of the ten-ask cap on every sweep and counted tail-only by \\u0060h9k status\\u0060 forever. The stream-state check still runs only on streams the plan already chose, so a bootstrap\\u0027s hundreds of held streams cost at most twenty reads a sweep. The attempt bump is staged before the broadcast so the count and the envelope land in the one commit \\u0060MessageOutbox.QueueAsync\\u0060 makes: a recorded attempt is always one that was actually asked. **The status pane.** \\u0060EventCatchUpPane\\u0060 composes plain lines rather than printing, the same split \\u0060ThroughputPane\\u0060 draws, so the wording is assertable without a terminal: the outstanding asks oldest first, then every request a decline closed inside 24 hours as \\u0060declined by \\u003Cnode\\u003E at \\u003Ctime\\u003E (\\u003Creason\\u003E)\\u0060 with the other declining members counted rather than listed, then \\u0060catch-up holds N streams tail-only, M given up after 3 asks\\u0060. A day is the window because that is the span over which somebody is still asking why a task they saw referenced this morning is not here. The reason itself is a string another node wrote, so the pane flattens its control characters to spaces and bounds its length before printing: the console renderer escapes Spectre markup but not a newline or an ANSI escape sequence, either of which would break the pane\\u0027s own line structure or restyle everything under it. The stored decline keeps the reason verbatim; this is a rule about printing, not about what was observed. The pane\\u0027s own \\u0060Describe\\u0060 is shared by the outstanding and declined lines so the two can never word the same ask differently. **Two false sentences corrected.** \\u0060h9k task pull\\u0060 said a broadcast \\u0022stays outstanding until some member\\u0027s answer applies here\\u0022, which stopped being true in v0.10.5 and is what sent a human back to re-run a command against an ask that had already been refused hours earlier; it now names the decline too, and points at the status line that reports it. **Tests.** Unit, database-free: the decline list (node, time, reason recorded; one entry per node; a repeat refreshes only the reason; a blank reason is labelled rather than invented), the pane\\u0027s whole wording including the day window, the silence on a request whose closing decline was never recorded, and a peer\\u0027s reason flattened of the control characters a terminal would otherwise obey, and the plan\\u0027s dedupe, cap, cooldown, three-attempt stop, deferred give-up and settle window, that last one stated as two hundred tails held two seconds ago minting nothing, which is the bootstrap case. Integration, against real Postgres: the held-tail ask end to end through three attempts with a decline closing each one, proving the outstanding guard, the cooldown, the counts landing on the records, the status counts while the ask stands, the give-up landing on the sweep after the last ask and only once, and no fourth ask; a held record whose stream exists locally handed back for replay rather than asked about; a tail re-served without its genesis leaving the ask bookkeeping and the original hold time untouched; that same residue replayed and deleted through the inbox; and the existing broadcast-decline test extended to prove the node and the time survive the round trip.
